Comment 6. Typically, a lower current density at the same voltage would be more favorable
for the device. However, compared to the control device, the TDFA device exhibits a higher
current density at the same voltage. This is abnormal compared to quantum dots based LEDs.
What causes this difference?
Reply: Typically, a lower current density at the same voltage is considered a positive
indicator of device optimization. A higher current density at the same voltage is not
generally a standard target for QLED optimization; however, it can be an intermediate result
of a more aggressive optimization strategy. Its ultimate value depends entirely on the
external quantum efficiency (EQE) performance, in which our case shows a significant
improvement.
We attribute this difference to the introduction of the TDFA method, which reduces
voids within the nanoplate (quantum well, QW) layer. In the device’s off-state region (< 2
V), these voids may penetrate multiple layers, allowing direct contact between adjacent
transport layers and causing leakage current. At the same voltage, this leakage current
increases the total current but represents non-radiative current that does not contribute to
light emission. In the on-state region (> 2 V), the charge transport pathways are disrupted
because the voids break the continuity of the QW network. This forces carriers to detour or
tunnel/jump across the voids, increasing the tortuosity of the path and thus the resistance,
leading to a reduction in current density and total current at the same voltage.
Overall, TDFA reduces leakage current in the off-state region and improves charge
carrier balance after turn-on. Additionally, the TDFA emissive layer is relatively thinner and
denser. Therefore, in the on-state region (> 2 V), the TDFA device enhances charge transport
pathways, allowing higher current flow at the same applied voltage.
We have now clarified these details in the revised manuscript (Page 14) as following.
The TDFA device in the conducting region exhibits higher current density, which can be
attributed to its relatively thinner, pinhole-free emissive layer that enhances charge transport
pathways, allowing greater current flow at the same applied voltage49.

## Paper

## Abstract

Colloidal quantum well-based light-emitting diodes are highly promising for electroluminescent applications owing to their high fraction of horizontally aligned transition dipole moments, but scalable fabricating their films with dominant horizontal dipole orientation for electroluminescent devices remain major challenges. Here, we utilize a two-phase driving flat arrangement strategy combined with Langmuir–Schaefer technology to create compact colloidal quantum well films with predominantly horizontal dipole alignment. The interfacial driving force between the two liquid phases facilitates the formation of uniform, densely packed films, which exhibit 90% horizontal dipole alignment, yielding a light extraction efficiency of 35.8%. The resulting devices achieve (4 mm2) an external quantum efficiency of 25.5%, a maximum luminance of 59,620 cd m−2, and outstanding operational stability (T95 @100 cd m−2 > 16,233 h). Moreover, this technique enables scalable fabrication of uniform colloidal quantum well films (100 cm2), maintaining luminance above 60,000 cd m−2 in 4 cm2 devices, indicating industrial feasibility.

---

## Introduction

Colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) have attracted considerable attention as next-generation light-emitting materials due to their tunable emission, ultranarrow linewidths, near-unity photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs), and exceptional stability1–8. Their quasi-two-dimensional structure imposes strong vertical quantum confinement while preserving delocalized in-plane excitons, yielding oriented transition dipole moments (TDMs) and enhanced light outcoupling, with theoretical EQEs approaching ~40%—well above conventional emitters9,10. The first CdSe CQW-based LEDs reported by Chen et al. in 2014 demonstrated an external quantum efficiency (EQE) below 1% and moderate brightness levels, highlighting the early-stage limitations of CQW device performance11. In recent years, CQW-based LEDs have developed rapidly. A notable improvement was realized in 2019, when Kelestemur et al. demonstrated CdSe/CdS/CdZnS heterostructured CQW LEDs with nearly 10% EQE12. In 2020, subsequent optimization of the device configuration, particularly the adoption of an inverted architecture with CdSe/CdZnS CQWs, enabled Liu et al. to achieve an EQE approaching 19%13. In 2024, further enhancement was realized by Ba et al., who introduced gradient-alloyed CdSe/CdZnS CQWs, achieving LEDs with up to 22% EQE14. Most recently, Zeng et al. reported core/crown/shell CdSe/CdSeS/CdZnS nanoplatelets exhibiting 100% PLQY and exceptional thermal stability, enabling LEDs with a record EQE exceeding 30%15. The state-of-the-art EQE of CQW-based LEDs is progressing by leaps and bounds.

Despite impressive advances in EQEs, a major challenge persists in improving the performance of CQW-based LEDs is the low proportion of horizontally aligned TDMs. The TDMs critically determine the photon emission characteristics of semiconductors so that play a key role in enabling the high theoretical EQE of CQW-based LEDs. The orientation of the TDMs depends on the alignment of the CQWs within films16. However, the characteristics of the fixed TDMs in CQW films have not been fully exploited, and a significant gap remains between the current efficiency of CQW-based LEDs and their theoretical limit. The orientation of the TDMs with respect to the device’s electrode interface is particularly important for maximizing outcoupling efficiency and is therefore a key factor in improving LED performance. In general, horizontally oriented TDMs favor efficient light extraction, whereas vertically oriented TDMs lead to energy losses and lower device efficiency17. Currently, CQW films for LED devices are prepared by spin-coating. For spin coating, as the droplet spreads radially outward from the center, the centrifugal force increases proportionally with the radial distance from the rotation axis. This results in a dense accumulation of CQWs at the films center and voids near the films edges. Although inkjet printing involves direct droplet deposition of colloidal nanocrystal solutions onto the substrate surface to form films layer-by-layer, this method tends to induce a coffee-ring effect, leading to central voids and edge accumulation18,19. Both approaches above tend to cause a random distribution of CQWs, failing to achieve a high proportion of horizontally aligned TDMs. Recently, several strategies have been developed to improve horizontal alignment. Combining interfacial ligand engineering with controlled self-assembly, CQW films with record horizontal dipole ratios of 92% and 95% were successfully fabricated, enabling efficient light outcoupling and achieving device performances with EQEs of 18.1% and 26.9% (Supplementary Table 1), respectively20,21. Although these methods have successfully achieved precise control of dipole orientation in CQW films, challenges persist in extending such control to large areas, scaling up device fabrication, and cost efficiency.

In this work, we devise a two-phase driving flat arrangement (TDFA) strategy by utilizing Langmuir-Schaefer technology to create compact, ordered-aligned CQW films. The CQW solution dissolved in chloroform forms a uniform film on the ethylene glycol sub-phase. Van der Waals (VDW) interactions between the CQW ligands and sub-phase molecules, together with the stronger facet-dependent interactions of the wide surfaces, promote the horizontal alignment of CQWs on the sub-phase, while the interfacial driving force between the two phases further induces their compact packing. Subsequently, the film is transferred onto a hole-transport-layer-coated substrate via the horizontal dipping method, yielding a densely packed, horizontally aligned CQW film. This achieves an in-plane TDMs ratio of approximately 90%, leading to a high light extraction efficiency of 35.8%. The resulting CQW-based LEDs show a high EQE of 25.5% and a maximum luminance of 59,620 cd m−2. Additionally, at a luminance of 100 cd m−2, the device demonstrates a T95 operational lifetime exceeding 16,233 hours, showcasing exceptional stability. The scalable fabrication process enables the production of large-area, uniform photoluminescent films, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Notably, the TDFA technique also demonstrates scalable fabrication capabilities, which enables LEDs with a 4 cm2 active area to maintain a luminance of over 60,000 cd m−2.

---

## Results

Fabrication and formation mechanism of CQW films
The CQW films fabricated via the spin-coating process served as the control sample in this work. The liquid spreading process is predominantly governed by centrifugal force in the spin-coating (Fig. 1a), whereas the combined effects of viscous forces, surface tension, and air resistance significantly influence the spreading dynamics and films formation22–26. As the liquid droplets propagate radially outward from the center, the centrifugal force increases linearly with radial distance, creating a shear gradient that drives CQWs toward the substrate edges, resulting in central aggregation and edge depletion. Thus, this phenomenon leads to non-uniform films morphology characterized by a thicker central region and progressively thinner edges. Consequently, the CQWs deposited on the substrate by spin-coating exhibit random distribution, with dense stacking at the center and voids near the edges of the films.

To address the limitations of spin-coating (uneven thickness and random CQWs distribution), we devised the TDFA process as shown in Fig. 1b. The CQWs solution (CQWs dissolved in chlorobenzene solvent) is firstly deposited onto an ethylene glycol subphase. The spreading behavior is primarily governed by surface tension and viscous drag. Then the liquids with lower surface tension tend to spread over those with higher surface tension. Thus, the diffusion occurs at a constant linear rate, enabling the formation of a uniform thickness films27. The TDFA process remains remarkably resilient to minor temperature fluctuations; even when the subphase temperature is elevated to 30°C, the compact, horizontally aligned arrangement of CQWs within the film is preserved without discernible disruption (Supplementary Fig. 1). When CQWs approach the ethylene glycol subphase, VDW interactions emerge between the oleic acid chains (surface ligands of CQWs) and the ethylene glycol molecules. The strength of these interactions depends on crystallographic facets: the wider facets exhibit stronger interactions due to their larger contact area and higher density of interaction sites, while the narrower facets show weaker interactions owing to limited molecular contact points28. These facet-dependent VDW interactions promote the horizontal alignment of CQWs on the sub-phase. Meanwhile, the compact packing of CQW films arises from differences in solvent vapor pressure. Specifically, the contrast in saturated vapor pressures between the two phases generates distinct driving forces for film formation: chloroform favors the formation of compact, horizontally stacked films, whereas solvents with either higher or lower vapor pressures (e.g., n-heptane, octane, n-hexane) disrupt this stacking (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3, and Supplementary Table 1). Consequently, during the spreading of the CQWs solution on the subphase, the wider facets preferentially adhere to the ethylene glycol interface, driving the formation of compact and a horizontally aligned CQW films with improved uniformity.

Characterization and morphology of the CQW films
To validate this assembly mechanism, the characterization and morphology of the CQW films have been studied. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 4) reveals a random and uneven CQWs distribution in the control film, contrasting sharply with the flat, compact structure of the TDFA film. The TDFA film exhibits a compact film morphology, with the CQWs demonstrating an almost completely horizontal alignment (Fig. 2b). The average spacing of these CQWs is more compact, smaller than that of the control CQWs film. The small particles in the TEM images may stem from byproducts or secondary nucleation and can be reduced by purification (Supplementary Fig. 5)29,30. Photoluminescence (PL) mapping further highlights this disparity: the control film exhibits localized bright spots (yellow circles in Supplementary Fig. 6a) caused by CQWs aggregation, while the TDFA film shows uniform emission (Supplementary Fig. 6b)31. Statistical analysis of the PL intensity distribution (Fig. 2c, d) reveals a narrower intensity spread in the TDFA film, with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 5.7% extreme lower than that of the control film (31%). The CV is defined as the standard deviation-to-mean ratio, representing the relative dispersion of the data. Thus, this result demonstrates the excellent flatness for the TDFA film.

Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) measurements corroborate these findings, demonstrating a root-mean-square roughness (Rrms) of 0.79 nm for the TDFA film, significantly lower than the 3.37 nm observed for the control film (Fig. 2e, f). The AFM-Amplitude results exhibit the same trend as the height data, which indirectly confirms the consistency of the Height measurements (Fig. 2g, h). The small difference in roughness between the two samples can be attributed to the fact that AFM provides only a relative indication of orientation trends, rather than a direct measurement of the CQW long-axis length.

The cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy–high-angle annular dark-field (STEM-HAADF) image of the control and TDFA samples are shown in Supplementary Fig. 7a, Supplementary Fig. 7b, respectively. The results indicate that the control sample exhibits a CQWs layer thickness of approximately 16 nm, with randomly oriented CQWs and noticeable voids. In contrast, the TDFA sample forms a predominantly horizontally aligned structure with an average thickness of about 9 nm, demonstrating a compact, pore-free film and a significant improvement in the horizontal alignment of CQWs. Furthermore, AFM measurements of the film thickness for both control and TDFA samples corroborate that the measured CQWs layer thickness matches well with the cross-sectional observations (Supplementary Fig. 8). The above results are as expected, the perfectly flat, compact, neatly arranged horizontal CQW films have been achieved by TDFA strategy, displaying great potential for optoelectronic devices.

Colloidal quantum well orientation of the films
Although the TDFA film exhibits a compact and horizontally aligned arrangement of CQWs, the ratio of horizontal TDMs remains unverified. To address this, we employed grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) to investigate the orientation of the CQWs. GIWAXS enables precise analysis of crystal plane alignment on film surfaces32. By combining the X-ray diffraction (XRD) data (Supplementary Fig. 9) with Bragg’s law, we identified three distinct diffraction rings corresponding to the (111), (220), and (311) crystal planes, from the innermost to the outermost rings (Fig. 3a, b). It is well known that diffraction rings appearing as discrete spots indicate a preferred orientation of specific crystal planes within the film. The GIWAXS results show that, compared to the TDFA film, the control film exhibits brighter diffraction spots on the (111) and (311) rings, suggesting a higher degree of preferential orientation along these planes. In contrast, the TDFA film demonstrates weaker diffraction intensity in these directions33. Since the (111) plane typically represents the strongest diffraction peak in zinc blende-structured CQWs—and the (111) and (311) planes correspond to the side and edge facets of the CQWs—their presence is indicative of vertical or tilted orientations. Notably, the GIWAXS patterns for both films exhibit weak diffraction spots for the (111) and (311) planes, while the (220) plane shows strong, continuous diffraction intensity. This implies that the (220) facet, rather than the (111) or (311), is predominantly oriented parallel to the substrate, indicating that most CQWs are horizontally aligned34. Compared to the control film, the TDFA film exhibits a reduction in the (111) and (311) signals, which indirectly suggests fewer vertically oriented CQWs and a tendency toward enhanced horizontal alignment. Since GIWAXS reflects crystal lattice orientations rather than the macroscopic platelet arrangement, it provides only indirect evidence of CQWs alignment. Therefore, we employed polarization-resolved PL and back focal plane (BFP) analysis to further substantiate this orientation trend.

In addition, polarization holography reveals distinct differences in CQW alignment between the control and TDFA films (Supplementary Fig. 10). The control sample (blue curve) exhibits pronounced intensity variations across different polarization angles, indicating strong polarization-dependent behavior consistent with the presence of vertically oriented CQWs. The degree of polarization (DOP), defined as DOP=(Imax−Imin)/(Imax+Imin)16,35,36, is 0.353 for the control sample, while the TDFA film shows a significantly lower DOP of 0.196. This suggests that the spin-coating process induces random geometric distributions of CQWs, with a notable fraction adopting near-perpendicular orientations relative to the substrate. These vertically aligned CQWs contribute to diverse in-plane dipole orientations, thereby enhancing optical anisotropy and polarization sensitivity. In contrast, the TDFA sample (red curve) exhibits a smooth and uniform angular response, indicating consistent light intensity across polarization angles. This reduced polarization dependence implies a predominant in-plane alignment of CQWs parallel to the substrate surface, resulting in more isotropic photon emission. These results further confirm the effectiveness of the TDFA process in controlling film orientation and promoting horizontal alignment of CQWs.

The orientation of transition dipole moments (TDMs) in the CQW films was investigated using back focal plane (BFP) imaging. Local excitation with a 405 nm laser was applied to probe microscale regions of the films. The resulting BFP patterns and corresponding p-polarized line-cut profiles are shown in Fig. 3c. A key signature of in-plane oriented dipoles is the attenuation of p-polarized emission near kx=k0, where kx represents the in-plane wave vector and k0 the wave vector in free space16. Distinct optical characteristics were observed between the control and TDFA-treated films. The control sample exhibited a discernible p-polarized intensity around kx/k0 = 1, whereas the TDFA film displayed nearly no emission in this region. In contrast, for s-polarized emission at ky/k0 = 1, both films showed measurable signals, but the TDFA film exhibited markedly stronger intensity. The degree of horizontal dipole alignment was quantified by the horizontal dipole ratio, Θ=p∥/(p∥+p⊥), where p∥ and p⊥ denote the in-plane and out-of-plane contributions of the optical TDMs, respectively37,38. Fitting the experimental data (Fig. 3d) yielded Θ≈62% for the control film and Θ≈90% for the TDFA treated film, confirming a pronounced enhancement in horizontal alignment16,39. These findings reveal that light emission from the TDFA film originates predominantly from horizontally oriented CQWs. Moreover, multilayer structures fabricated via sequential TDFA deposition (two- and three-layer films) retained strong in-plane orientation (> 85%), demonstrating the robustness of this approach for constructing highly ordered CQW assemblies through a layer-by-layer process (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Simulation of light extraction of CQW-based LEDs
To validate the enhanced light extraction enabled by high-horizontal-TDM films, we conducted finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations40. Using layer-specific parameters (Supplementary Fig. 12), we modeled the outcoupling mechanism in the CQW-based LEDs (Supplementary Fig. 13). The schematic illustrates the light outcoupling mechanisms in the CQW-based LEDs under control and TDFA configurations. For the control device (left image), the photons emitted from the CQWs layer propagate through the device’s multilayer structure (e.g., ZnMgO and Al layers). The random orientation of horizontal TDMs within the CQWs causes emitted photons to undergo multiple internal reflections and scattering events, disrupting their propagation paths and resulting in suboptimal light extraction. In contrast, the TDFA device (right panel) features a well-ordered horizontal TDMs orientation induced by the TDFA process. This alignment enhances in-plane dipole–photon coupling and minimizes parasitic reflections and scattering losses. As a result, photons are more efficiently directed through the ZnMgO and Al layers, leading to significantly improved outcoupling efficiency.

To investigate the wavelength-dependent optical behavior of horizontally oriented dipoles across the visible spectrum, we employed two complementary simulation methods: the Dipole Power method and the Box method (Fig. 4a). The Dipole Power method calculates the radiation characteristics of an individual dipole emitter, making it well-suited for localized sources under simplified boundary conditions. In contrast, the Box method accounts for complex optical architectures with strict boundary constraints, enabling comprehensive modeling of system-wide phenomena such as photon propagation, scattering, and absorption41,42. The strong agreement between the two methods confirms the accuracy of our boundary condition parameterization and validates the reliability of the simulations. As shown in Fig. 4a, the simulated dipole power exhibits a monotonic decline with increasing wavelength, attributed to enhanced surface plasmon-polariton (SPP) resonance effects at shorter wavelengths (λ<50 nm)43. This trend aligns with the spectral dependence of metal-dielectric interfacial modes in multilayer optoelectronic systems. The simulated wavelength-resolved outcoupling efficiency (ηout), presented in Fig. 4b, indicates an efficiency of approximately 37.9% in the red spectral region (621 nm). The light-coupling efficiency varies significantly with wavelength, primarily because the physical mechanisms governing light–matter interactions are inherently highly wavelength-dependent44,45. Additionally, the simulated angular radiation profile (Fig. 4c) exhibits a Lambertian emission pattern, as evidenced by the symmetric intensity distribution about θ=0° (the optical axis)—a hallmark characteristic of ideal Lambertian emitters. Based on the measured horizontal dipole orientation ratios of 62% for the control configuration and 90% for the TDFA configuration, optical outcoupling simulations were conducted (Fig. 4d, e). The control configuration yielded a maximum ηout of 24.4%. In contrast, the TDFA configuration achieved a significantly higher ηout of 35.8% (Fig. 4f), primarily attributed to reduced optical losses stemming from improved dipole alignment and the suppression of interfacial SPP modes. The reduced ηout observed at CQW-to-electrode distances d>50 nm is attributed to increased propagation losses and enhanced optical absorption within the device’s constituent materials46. The EQE of the LEDs is equal to the product of internal quantum efficiency (IQE) and ηout. The higher ηout, the more internally generated photons can be efficiently extracted to the external environment, reducing optical losses and enhancing light output. This directly enhances the EQE of the LEDs.

Performance of CQW-based LEDs
We fabricated CQW-based LEDs and evaluated the angular variation of electroluminescence (EL) intensity for both the control and TDFA devices. Both devices exhibited Lambertian emission patterns, although the EL intensity curve of the TDFA device was slightly lower than that of the control (Fig. 5a). This discrepancy may be attributed to subtle differences in the alignment of the CQWs, which can modulate the angular distribution of EL. The Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage (CIE) coordinates of the EL peak is (0.675, 0.321), which is close to the Rec. 2020 standard for pure red emission (0.708, 0.292) (Supplementary Fig. 14). Figure 5b shows the normalized EL spectra, revealing no significant differences in peak positions or intensities between the two devices, thereby confirming that the TDFA preserves the original EL characteristics. Figure 5c presents the current density (J)–voltage (V)–luminance (L) characteristics. In the low-voltage regime (red box), the control device exhibited a significant leakage current, which was absent in the TDFA device. This is due to the uneven CQWs distribution and voids in the control film, whereas the horizontal alignment and compact morphology in the TDFA film suppress defect-mediated leakage current47,48, The TDFA device in the conducting region exhibits higher current density, which can be attributed to its relatively thinner, pinhole-free emissive layer that enhances charge transport pathways, allowing greater current flow at the same applied voltage49. As the voltage increased, the TDFA device rapidly reached peak luminance, demonstrating low-voltage, high-luminance performance that is advantageous for operational longevity. The current–voltage (J–V) characteristics of the single-carrier devices indicate that, compared to the control, the TDFA devices exhibit more balanced electron and hole density profiles under the same bias conditions. This balanced current density of electrons and holes suggests a potential advantage for device performance optimization and enhanced operational stability (Supplementary Fig. 15)50. The TDFA device achieved 25.5% peak EQE and 59,620 cd m−2 maximum luminance, surpassing the control device (19.83% EQE, 39,880 cd m−2) (Fig. 5d). Considering that the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of the TDFA film is 72%, this suggests that the ηout of the TDFA device is 35.5%, which is in good agreement with our theoretical simulations (Fig. 4).

To systematically evaluate the reproducibility of the TDFA process, we performed a statistical analysis of EQE measurements across 30 independently fabricated devices. As shown in Fig. 5e, the efficiency histogram exhibits a distribution with a mean value of 23.8%, confirming the exceptional process consistency of our approach. Device stability was assessed under accelerated aging conditions (initial luminance = 10,605 cd m−2) by continuously monitoring the luminance decay. The degradation kinetics were analyzed using the empirical relationship (L0)n × T95 = constant, where L₀ denotes initial luminance and n represents the acceleration factor51; in this case, n was approximately 1.88. Based on the measured T95 @10,000 cd m−2 ≈ 152 minutes (Fig. 5f), the extrapolated T95 @1,000 cd m−2 exceeds 214 hours and the extrapolated T95 @100 cd m−2 exceeds 16,233 hours, demonstrating the longest operational stability reported so far in CQW-based LEDs that reaches commercially viable levels52.

The TDFA method enables uniform large-area film formation while reducing solution consumption by 90% compared to the conventional spin-coating process, which typically requires excessive amounts of CQWs and results in non-uniform film morphology (Supplementary Fig. 16). To further demonstrate the scalability of the TDFA process, we fabricated a 10 × 10 cm2 large-area CQWs film (Fig. 5g). The resulting film exhibited a highly uniform morphology without the edge coverage deficiencies commonly observed in conventional methods, thereby validating the technical feasibility of TDFA for scalable LED manufacturing. Furthermore, we successfully fabricated large-area CQW-based LEDs with dimensions of 2 × 2 cm2, achieving luminance levels exceeding 60,000 cd m−2 (Fig. 5h, Supplementary Fig. 17). Compared to small-area devices, the reduction of EQE in large-area devices may arise from increased series resistance, a higher probability of defects, inadequate thermal management, non-ideal charge transport, size-dependent optical outcoupling and cavity effects, among other factors53–56. The large-area device at turn-on voltage under low luminance illustrate the uniform emission, verifying the feasibility of the TDFA for large-scale manufacture of CQW-based LEDs. (Supplementary Fig. 18). This scalability highlights the strong potential of the TDFA process for industrial-scale LED production.

## Methods

Materials
The poly (3,4-ethylene dioxythiophene) / poly (styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) was purchased from Xi’an Polymer Light Technology Corp, poly((9,9-dioctylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl)-alt-(9-(2-ethylhexyl)-carbazole-3,6-diyl)) (PF8CZ) was purchased from Polymer Light Technology Inc. Sodium tetradecanoate (99.99%), Cadmium nitrate tetrahydrate (99.99%), Cadmium acetate dihydrate (99.99%), Selenium powder (99.99%), Anhydrous cadmium acetate (99.99%), Zinc acetate (99.99%), Oleamine (90%), 1-Octadecylene (90%), Octanethiol (99.99%), Methanol (99.99%), Ethanol (99%), N-hexane (99.99%) and Methyl acetate (99.99%) were purchased from Aladin. Oleic acid (90%) was purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Ethylene glycol (99%), chlorobenzene (99.).

Syntheses of colloidal quantum wells
Cadmium myristate (567 mg, 1 mmol), selenium powder (24 mg, 0.5 mmol), and octadecene (50 mL) are placed into a 100 mL three-necked flask. After three argon–vacuum exchange cycles, the mixture is degassed at 100°C for 1 h. The temperature is then elevated to 200°C, at which point a methanolic solution of cadmium acetate monohydrate is injected once the solution turns orange. The reaction is maintained at 240°C for approximately 0.2 h, after which 1 mL of oleic acid is added while cooling to room temperature. For purification, the crude product is washed sequentially with hexane and methyl acetate, centrifuged at 8,000 rpm for 0.083 h, redispersed in hexane, and centrifuged again at 10,000 rpm for 0.017 h. The optical absorption spectrum is subsequently recorded using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer to determine the position of the first excitonic absorption peak. A colloidal CdSe CQW dispersion (1 mL, optical density=30 at the first excitonic transition), cadmium acetate anhydrous (23 mg, 0.1 mmol), zinc acetate anhydrous (73 mg, 0.4 mmol), oleic acid (1 mL), and octadecene (10 mL) are loaded into a 50 mL three-necked flask. The mixture is degassed at 100°C for 0.2 h, after which 0.5 mL of oleylamine is swiftly introduced. The temperature is then raised to 300°C. Octanethiol is introduced continuously at a rate of 1.5 mmol h-1 when the reaction temperature reaches 180°C, and the rate is adjusted to 0.78 mmol h-1 once the temperature increases to 240°C. After the entire amount of octanethiol is delivered, the reaction is maintained at 300°C for an additional 0.5 h before cooling to ambient temperature naturally.

Synthesis of ZnMgO nanoparticles
Zn0.875Mg0.125O nanoparticles were synthesized through a solution-phase precipitation method. Initially, a precursor solution containing precisely controlled stoichiometric ratios of zinc acetate dihydrate (Zn(OAc)2·2H2O, 5.25 mmol) and magnesium acetate tetrahydrate (Mg(OAc)2·4H2O, 0.75 mmol) in anhydrous dimethyl sulfoxide (60 mL) was prepared. This was subsequently mixed with a separately formulated ethanol solution (20 mL) of tetramethylammonium hydroxide pentahydrate (TMAH, 10 mmol) under ambient conditions with continuous magnetic stirring for 1 hour. The resultant colloidal suspension underwent thorough purification via centrifugal separation (6000 rpm, 10 min cycles) with ethanol/acetone (3:1) to remove ionic byproducts, ultimately yielding monodispersed Zn0.875Mg0.125O nanoparticles stabilized in ethanol medium.

Control device fabrication
The device structure consists of indium tin oxide (ITO) glass / PEDOT:PSS / PF8CZ / CQWs / ZnMgO / aluminum (Al). The CQW-LED was fabricated on an ITO-coated glass substrate with a sheet resistance of approximately 20 Ω sq−1. The ITO substrate was sequentially cleaned via ultrasonication in deionized water (15 min), acetone (15 min), and ethanol (15 min), followed by ultraviolet (UV) ozone treatment for 15 min to enhance its work function. A layer of PEDOT:PSS (AI4083) was spin-coated onto the substrate at 5000 rpm and annealed at 140°C for 15 min. The ITO/PEDOT substrate was then transferred into a nitrogen glovebox, where a PF8CZ layer was spin-coated at 3000 rpm (12 mg ml−1 in chlorobenzene) and annealed at 150°C for 30 min. Subsequently, the CQW layer was spin-coated at 3000 rpm (30 mg ml−1 in octane) and annealed at 90°C for 10 min. A ZnMgO layer was then spin-coated at 2000 rpm (30 mg ml−1 in ethanol) and annealed at 60°C for 30 min. Finally, the sample was loaded into a custom-built high-vacuum deposition chamber to thermally evaporate a 100 nm thick aluminum cathode, defining a 4 mm diameter active emission area.

Two-phase driving flat arrangement device fabrication
The device structure consists of indium tin oxide (ITO) glass / PEDOT:PSS / PF8CZ / CQWs / ZnMgO / aluminum (Al). The CQW-LED was fabricated on an ITO-coated glass substrate with a sheet resistance of approximately 20 Ω sq−1. The ITO substrate was sequentially cleaned via ultrasonication in deionized water (15 min), acetone (15 min), and ethanol (15 min), followed by ultraviolet (UV) ozone treatment for 15 min to enhance its work function. A layer of PEDOT:PSS (AI4083) was spin-coated onto the substrate at 5,000 rpm and annealed at 140°C for 15 min. The ITO/PEDOT substrate was transferred into a nitrogen glovebox, where a PF8CZ layer was spin-coated at 3,000 rpm (12 mg ml−1 in chlorobenzene) and annealed at 150°C for 30 min. For the CQW layer deposition, an ethylene glycol subphase solution was first poured into a horizontal solution trough. Drop an appropriate concentration of CQW chloroform solution into the ethylene glycol subphase to form a horizontally oriented CQW film. The ITO/PEDOT/PF8CZ substrate was carefully immersed into the trough, and the CQW film was transferred onto the substrate via the two-phase driving flat arrangement (TDFA) method. Subsequently, a ZnMgO layer was spin-coated at 2000 rpm (30 mg ml−1 in ethanol) and annealed at 60°C for 30 min. Finally, the sample was loaded into a custom-built high vacuum deposition chamber to thermally evaporate a 100 nm thick aluminum cathode, defining a 4 mm diameter active emission area.

CQW-LEDs characterizations
The structural characteristics of the CQWs were investigated using a JEOL JEM−2010 transmission electron microscope, operated at 200 kV. This instrument provides high-resolution imaging capabilities, essential for detailed morphological analysis. Crystallographic analysis of the CQWs was performed using a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer. This system is designed for comprehensive X-ray diffraction applications, including phase identification and microstructure analysis. Current density–voltage–luminance (J–V–L) measurements were conducted with a Keithley 2400 source meter and a Keithley 6485 picoammeter, coupled with a Si photodetector (Newport 818-UV). Luminance calibration was achieved using a Minolta CS-100 Chroma Meter under ambient conditions. Electroluminescence (EL) spectra were recorded employing an Ocean Optics USB4000 spectrometer in conjunction with the Keithley 2400 power supply.

PL mapping measurement
The fluorescence images of single particles were measured using the 40× objective lens with N.A. of 0.95, which was built on the laser scanning confocal microscope (Nikon A1, inverted microscope). The excitation wavelength was 405 nm.

Polarization degree measurement
The measurement was performed using a fluorescence spectrometer (F-380). The prepared thin film samples were placed in the sample holder, and a polarizer was inserted between the fluorescence spectrometer and the sample holder. The fluorescence spectral intensity was recorded, after which the polarizer was rotated to different angles and the fluorescence intensity was measured accordingly.

Back focal plane imaging measurement
BFP imaging was employed to map the angular distribution of emitted light. A 405 nm continuous-wave laser was used to excite photoluminescence in a nanosheet/coverslip/oil trilayer structure. Emission was collected via a high-NA oil-immersion objective (UPlanSApo 100×, NA 1.44). The objective’s back focal plane was projected onto a Princeton Instruments HRS-300 imaging spectrograph through a 50 mm lens system, enabling polarization-resolved detection to differentiate in-plane and out-of-plane dipole orientations.

GIWAXS measurement
GIWAXS measurements were performed at the SAXS beamline of the Xeuss 2.0 system (Xenocs, France). The collected data were analyzed using SGTools to extract structural information of the CQWs in thin-film configurations.

Refractive index measurement
The refractive index of films in CQW-LED was measured by an ellipsometer (HORIBA France SAS Spectroscopic Ellipsometer, Eceshi Company).

TDFD computation
In this study, we employed finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations to investigate the photonic propagation characteristics of cascade quantum well (CQW)-based devices.

Data availability
All data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper and its Supplementary files. Any additional information related to the study is available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

further suppresses coupling efficiency. Therefore, the contrast between high coupling
efficiency at shorter wavelengths and its sharp decline in the longer-wavelength regime, as

indicator of device optimization. A higher current density at the same voltage is not
generally a standard target for QLED optimization; however, it can be an intermediate result
of a more aggressive optimization strategy. Its ultimate value depends entirely on the

We attribute this difference to the introduction of the TDFA method, which reduces
voids within the nanoplate (quantum well, QW) layer. In the device’s off-state region (< 2

transport layers and causing leakage current. At the same voltage, this leakage current
increases the total current but represents non-radiative current that does not contribute to
light emission. In the on-state region (> 2 V), the charge transport pathways are disrupted
because the voids break the continuity of the QW network. This forces carriers to detour or
tunnel/jump across the voids, increasing the tortuosity of the path and thus the resistance,
leading to a reduction in current density and total current at the same voltage.
Overall, TDFA reduces leakage current in the off-state region and improves charge
carrier balance after turn-on. Additionally, the TDFA emissive layer is relatively thinner and
denser. Therefore, in the on-state region (> 2 V), the TDFA device enhances charge transport
pathways, allowing higher current flow at the same applied voltage.

Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. This method has made true advancement
for the fabrication of CQW based LEDs as following:
For the fabrication of large-area CQW thin films, achieving highly horizontally oriented
TDMs is relatively straightforward, which offers significant advantages over conventional
methods such as spin-coating. Furthermore, common approaches rely on self-assembly to
achieve high TDMs and thus high device performance. Here, we demonstrate a novel
method that attains both high TDMs and excellent device performance, while also offering
advantages for the fabrication of large-area films, enabling the successful production of
large-area devices.
A previously reported work (Advanced Materials (DOI: 10.1002/adma.202305382) and
Small (DOI: 10.1002/smll.202206582)) demonstrated remarkable progress by designing a
spin-coating-assisted self-assembly strategy to obtain highly oriented TDMs and efficient
CQW-LEDs, thereby overcoming the traditional orientation limitations of spin coating.
However, when it comes to preparing large-area films with high orientation, the spin-coating
process still suffers from inherent drawbacks—most notably its poor scalability, which
makes it unsuitable for uniform large-area deposition. For instance, as shown in the 10 cm
× 10 cm film in our work (Fig. 5, Extended Data Fig.15), the TDFA method readily produces
highly horizontally oriented TDM films, whereas spin coating cannot achieve such complete
coverage.
In comparison, techniques such as inkjet printing and drop-casting can indeed produce
large-area films, but the orientation of CQWs cannot be precisely controlled using these
methods. Therefore, whether by spin coating, inkjet printing, or drop-casting, it remains
very challenging to simultaneously achieve both large area and high orientation. More
importantly, spin coating suffers from extremely low material utilization, typically only
1~5%. In contrast, the theoretical material utilization of our TDFA method can reach up to
90%. This advantage is particularly critical for expensive materials such as CQWs, as it
significantly reduces cost and provides a viable approach for future industrialization. We
also successfully fabricated large-area LEDs using TDFA method, achieving a luminance
of over 60,000 cd/m2, which demonstrates the potential of TDFA for large-area LED
applications.
